title: RALFuzz: Execution-Aware and Risk-Aware LLM-Assisted Fuzz Harness Generation for C Library APIs
authors: Jinyu Zhou; Zitong Zhu; Yuqi Xiong; Zhijie Li; Jianxi Wu
abstract: Fuzzing C libraries depends on carefully constructed harnesses. They must initialise the target library, prepare valid and malformed inputs, invoke the target API, and release resources correctly. Writing them manually is labour-intensive and limits fuzzing across large API surfaces. We present RALFuzz, an open-source Python command-line toolchain for automated fuzz harness generation and evolutionary mutation for C library APIs. RALFuzz addresses the harness-construction bottleneck with a two-stage workflow: seed construction guided by execution context and risk information, followed by evolutionary mutation. Execution awareness grounds prompts and validation in concrete build, call-context, and cleanup requirements, while risk awareness steers generated probes toward API-specific hazards. The tool combines lightweight API discovery, heuristic risk profiling, LLM-assisted C harness generation, compiler-grounded validation, sanitizer instrumentation, and structured artifact archival.In an illustrative run on cJSON_Parse, RALFuzz generated six validated seed harnesses from six attempts, and expanded them into 32 accepted harnesses spanning 12 distinct behaviour signatures, without manual harness editing. These results show RALFuzz turning LLM-based C harness generation into a reproducible, compiler-checkable testing workflow.

title: Harness Engineering for LLM Agents: A Survey of Harness Component Taxonomy, Evaluation, and Model–Harness Coevolution
authors: Jinzhe Li; Yuan Wu; Yi Chang
abstract: As large language model-driven autonomous agents are increasingly deployed in real-world long-horizon, open-environment tasks, foundation models expose systematic capability gaps in context retention, reliable tool invocation, persistent state management, and multi-step execution robustness. We understand the agent harness as the external execution support structure built around the model and treat it as a distinct performance lever that complements base model capability, positioning harness engineering as a growing area of research and engineering practice. Grounded in the scaffolding perspective from developmental psychology, we structure the field along three nested levels of analysis. At the structural level, we develop a unified taxonomy of harness components, mapping them to the specific capability gaps they compensate for and to their coupling with the core agent loop. At the fit level, we articulate a two-stage evaluation logic that distinguishes native model capability-gap diagnosis from assessments of compensation effectiveness and net benefit, and unpack the inherent multi-objective tradeoffs shaping harness design. At the dynamic level, we delineate the bidirectional coevolution mechanism between models and harnesses, explaining the shifting functional boundary where routine capability-bearing support migrates inward into model weights while constraint-bearing governance functions remain external. By synthesizing studies that are currently scattered across adjacent areas, we provide an organizing framework for understanding LLM agent harnesses in relation to the capability gaps they address. We further discuss open challenges and future directions in harness design, evaluation, and model--harness coevolution.

title: Harness Resilience: From LLM Availability to Toolchain Continuity in Agentic AI Engineering
authors: John Cheung
abstract: By early 2026, the practical value of artificial intelligence in software engineering is no longer determined solely by the reliability of the underlying large language model (LLM). Increasingly, productivity depends on an execution harness: the surrounding runtime of prompts, tools, sandboxes, permissions, memory, repositories, connectors, model-routing policies, observability, and user-interface affordances that turn a model into an operational coding or general-purpose agent. Popular systems such as Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor-like development environments, and general agents such as Manus demonstrate that the “AI product” is not only a model but a socio-technical toolchain. This paper argues that AI resilience must therefore be extended into harness resilience: the ability of an engineering team to continue safe and effective work when a preferred AI agent harness changes behavior, loses access, degrades, is rate-limited, is withdrawn from a plan, suffers a security incident, or becomes unavailable. Using an illustrative X.com post by Peter Gostev about a Claude Code user being humorously shown as opted out after a code-quality review, this paper motivates a broader resilience agenda: portability of context, tool abstraction, reproducible agent workflows, fallback harnesses, audit trails, and human recovery procedures. The paper contributes a reference architecture, a failure-mode taxonomy, measurable resilience objectives, a connector threat model, and an evaluation plan that turns the concept from a practice guide into a testable engineering framework.

title: Security Knowledge Distillation for Enhancing LLM Safety in Code Generation Authors
authors: Sarah Mitchell; Jason Li; Daniel Thompson
abstract: We propose a distillation framework that transfers secure coding expertise into a compact model trained using expert demonstrations, static-analysis labels, and secure patterns. The distilled model (7B parameters) achieves 83% security compliance, nearly matching GPT-4's 89% performance while requiring significantly less compute. Evaluated across CWE-20, CWE-78, CWE-89, the distilled model reduces injection vulnerabilities by 62% relative to baseline models. This work demonstrates that targeted distillation can teach smaller models to respect security best practices.

title: Security Unit Test Generation for LLM-Produced Code Using Constraint-Based Mutation Authors
authors: Sophie Maes; Jonas De Wilde; Liam Verhoeven
abstract: We propose an automated unit test generator designed to reveal security weaknesses in LLM-generated programs. The system applies constraint-based input mutation combined with vulnerability oracles for injection, overflow, and authentication flaws. Evaluated on 1,500 code samples generated by five LLMs, the framework detects 41% more security faults than fuzzing-based test generators. Code coverage increases by 22%, and time-to-bug discovery is reduced by half. The results show the value of pairing LLM outputs with adversarial unit-test synthesis.

title: ASG-LLM: An LLM-Based Pipeline for Automated Scraping Code Generation in Security-Sensitive Environments
authors: Sokheang Chan; Naro Vorn; Vungsovanreach Kong; Chang Kue Seok; Jong-Hyun Kim; Dr. Anand Nayyar; Tae-Kyung KIM
abstract: Automating interactions with security-sensitive web services remains difficult due to dynamic frontends, session-bound tokens, and undocumented parameter-generation logic. Traditionally, developers must manually analyze captured traffic, hypothesize parameter-generation routines, and iteratively test internally defined functions until the interaction succeeds. We propose ASG-LLM, an execution grounded pipeline that generates scraping modules from a single successful browser session trace. ASG-LLM captures full HTTP(S) traffic, removes irrelevant requests through multi-stage filtering, and constructs a dependency-aware representation of the core interaction flow. When security-critical parameters cannot be reconstructed from the trace alone, the FUNC Retriever identifies a small set of reusable internal function descriptions using HyDE-guided selective retrieval, enabling the LLM to select compatible parameter-generation routines based on behavioral similarity rather than keyword matching, without exposing proprietary implementation code. Generated modules are executed in a controlled environment and iteratively repaired using structured failure feedback. ASG-LLM was evaluated on representative banking and public-sector portals. In our case studies, ASG-LLM reduces developer effort by cutting traffic analysis and basic code implementation from hours to minutes and reducing security-handling effort from a full-day task to a couple of hours. At the model level, HyDE-based selective retrieval improves internal function recommendation accuracy from 30% to 70% Top-1 and from 60% to 90% Top-3 compared with a full-context baseline. These results suggest that combining trace grounding, selective retrieval, and execution-time validation is a promising direction for robust web automation in security-constrained environments.

title: Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Automation for Software Test Script Generation
authors: Srikanth Kavuri
abstract: With the rapid evolution of software systems and the growing complexity of their testing needs, test automation has become more essential than ever within the software development life cycle (SDLC). Yet, despite advances in tooling, the process of creating test scripts still tends to be manual, time-consuming, and highly dependent on both programming skills and domain expertise. In this study, we explore a practical approach that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) including GPT-based models to automate the generation of test scripts directly from natural language software requirements or user stories. The method combines prompt engineering with lightweight fine-tuning and the use of domain-specific data to generate executable test cases. We applied this framework across a range of real-world software projects and used popular testing tools like Selenium and PyTest to assess performance in terms of script accuracy, maintainability, and the overall reduction in developer workload. Our findings show that LLM-generated tests significantly reduce manual effort and produce results that are close to human-written scripts in terms of coverage and correctness. Overall, the approach offers a flexible solution for integrating AI-powered test generation into CI/CD pipelines and could mark a step forward in how teams approach software testing in agile environments.

title: Harness-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agents: Systems, Benchmarks, and Protocols
authors: Ahmed Y. Radwan; Athanasios V. Vasilakos; Shaina Raza
abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly combine model capabilities with memory, tools, and execution control to perform tasks across diverse environments. As research pursues more general intelligence, recent results highlight the importance of the agent harness: changing the execution system around a fixed model can alter performance and even reverse model rankings. Yet inconsistent reporting of harness configurations, resource budgets, and scoring procedures makes benchmark results difficult to interpret and compare. This survey reviews the development of agent harnesses and introduces a four-factor evaluation framework comprising the model, harness, environment, and evaluator, alongside the protocol under which they are tested. We map representative systems and benchmarks to this framework, examining evidence on task performance, reliability, safety, and human oversight. We distinguish what existing comparisons establish from effects that remain entangled, and provide factor-level reporting guidance to support consistent and reproducible evaluation. Finally, we identify research directions in adaptive harnesses, resource-aware comparisons, and the generalization of harness effects across models and environments.

title: HELM: Harness Engineering for LLM Decision-Making Agents in Emergency Operations and Management
authors: Abhinav Shrestha; Liming Lu; Junkang Xu; Chao Fan
abstract: Emergency dispatch operations impose substantial cognitive demands on dispatchers, requiring them to maintain situational awareness of evolving incidents, track available resources, and make high-stakes decisions for extended periods. These demands motivate the development of decision-support tools that reduce cognitive burden. While LLMs show strong capacities for reasoning and contextual understanding, effectively harnessing their capabilities requires system designs that specify how models perceive operational context and interact with changing environments. To address this gap, we propose HELM, Harness Engineering for LLM decision-making agents in Emergency Operations and Management, an operational harness that embeds LLMs as decision-making agents within a dynamic emergency management simulation. HELM consists of two modules: structured state observation, which preprocesses incident and unit information into a decision-relevant state representation, and an event-driven interaction mechanism, which invokes model reasoning only at operationally meaningful decision points. We evaluate HELM against baseline models across multiple LLMs in a simulated 911 emergency dispatch environment. Results show that HELM improves operational performance by up to 400% over ReAct by improving spatial awareness and reducing inefficient dispatch decisions. Specifically, HELM enables models to allocate limited response units more effectively across concurrent incidents while avoiding excessive prioritization of high-severity incidents. We also find that model selection for time-constrained operational environments requires balancing reasoning capability with response latency, since stronger reasoning does not necessarily translate into better outcomes when slower responses limit the effectiveness of actions. Overall, HELM demonstrates how engineering LLM harnesses can improve decision-support systems for emergency operations and management.

title: Harness engineering enables a multi-agent LLM system to generate cross-domain hypotheses beyond single-investigator reach
authors: Keiro Watanabe; Takeshi Omasa
abstract: Abstract                   Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate scientific hypotheses, and a more capable model is widely assumed to drive output quality. We tested this with a biology-focused multi-agent system coupling an LLM to five Model Context Protocol servers exposing 66 external tools. Upgrading the Synthesizer and Critic from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Opus 4.8 initially appeared to improve quality, count, and reliability. Under a fully matched harness (identical prompts, schema, hypothesis count, and queries), the differences vanished: scores were indistinguishable on an iPSC-reprogramming task and favoured Sonnet 4.6 on a CHO cell-line-engineering task (18.4 vs 17.4; Welch t = 2.89, p < 0.05). The dominant, controllable driver of quality is therefore the prompting harness, not the model tier. We then introduce the ABCD-Stack (contract-gated prompting, diversity-first generation, adversarial refinement, and cross-family evaluation), which builds these properties in as architecture and shifts outputs toward explicitly falsifiable, causally framed hypotheses beyond the reach of a single-domain investigator. The hypotheses are falsifiable by construction but not yet experimentally validated.

title: Harness Engineered LLM Agents for Material Science: A Case Study on Perovskite Materials with Machine Learning and Materials Project
authors: Lei Zhang; Tianle Wang
abstract: The integration of AI agents into materials science has gained noteworthy momentum in recent years. A fundamental challenge remains how to balance fully autonomous LLM-driven agent risking unpredictable or physically impossible results, against rigid and unadaptable standard operating procedures. This study applies Harness strategy as a feasible approach to designing agent interfaces for materials science, with a case study on perovskite materials using machine learning algorithms and crystal structure tools. The proposed agent framework with the harness concept replaces hard-coded operations with LLM-driven adaptive decisions across subclass assignment, feature selection, model selection, modelling scheduling, and result interpretation. Eleven machine learning regressors are evaluated under two conditions: without Harness (single pooled model) and with Harness (subclass-specific models with sample-count-weighted evaluation). Results demonstrate that Harness engineering improves machine learning model accuracies of these perovskite materials on across the machine learning model families based on retrieved perovskite data at the first-principles level in this specific case. This study provides a platform to transform AI agents into harnessed and reliable collaborators for materials science research.

title: LLM-based multi-agent system for generation and evolution of CodeQL static analysis rules for C/C++
authors: Anastasia B. Arkhipova; Eva D. Azeeva
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of ensuring security for C/C++ software systems, where static code analysis serves as a key tool for vulnerability detection but remains costly to maintain due to the complexity of developing rules and taint specifications. Existing approaches are analyzed: industrial static analyzers (Svace, Irbis), IFDS analysis, ML/NN-based solutions, and hybrid schemes involving large language models (LLMs) used for warning filtering, code generation, and automatic rule synthesis (QLPro, KNighter, CodePatchLLM). It is shown that direct use of LLMs as standalone vulnerability detectors yields high recall but is accompanied by a significant number of false positives and hallucinations. As an alternative, a multi-agent module for the SAST tool CodeQL, tailored for C/C++, is proposed. It leverages LLMs for the generation, validation, and evolution of rules in the QL query language within a closed loop of "generation, verification, refinement, filtering, ranking". The system architecture is described, featuring generator, validator, refiner, filter, and ranker agents, whose orchestration is implemented using LangGraph and PostgreSQL. Rule validation is performed against CodeQL databases Juliet, SARD, and real-world projects, with calculation of metrics including Precision, Recall, F1, FPR, and Specificity, and consideration of CVSS scores. This enables the selection of rules of acceptable quality and reduces the burden on developers through automated evolution of the rule base.

title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness
authors: Yunbei Zhang; Janet Wang; Yingqiang Ge; Weijie Xu; Jihun Hamm; Chandan K. Reddy
abstract: This position paper argues that, for long-horizon tasks evaluated across models with comparable frontier capability, the agent execution harness, namely the infrastructure layer that governs context construction, tool interaction, orchestration, and verification around a language model, is often a stronger determinant of agent performance than the model it wraps. We formalize and defend the Binding Constraint Thesis: in this regime, performance variance is governed more by harness configuration than by model choice, and current evaluation protocols therefore systematically misattribute harness-level gains to model improvements. We support this thesis along three lines. First, a control-theoretic formalization treats the harness as the controller of a closed-loop dynamical system and the LLM as the stochastic policy it governs, which explains why small harness changes can produce performance shifts that exceed those obtained by substituting one model for another. Second, published benchmarks, industry deployments, and a controlled variance decomposition show that harness-induced variance can substantially exceed model-induced variance, including cases of model ranking reversal. Third, we propose a harness-aware evaluation framework with a disclosure standard and a variance decomposition protocol. Until harness specifications are disclosed, leaderboard comparisons for long-horizon agents should be treated as incomplete and potentially misleading.
